bullets: Sorting lemon juice, vinegar, soap and baking soda on one number line: the pH scale, and what happens when an acid meets an alkali
slides.heading: Acids, bases and salts
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we sort acids and alkalis on the pH scale, explain pH with ions, neutralise an acid step by step, name the salt, and read the jump on a titration curve.

bullets: Read the pH scale from 0 to 14 and explain pH in terms of hydrogen and hydroxide ions
Describe neutralisation as H+ and OH- ions forming water, name the salt from the acid, and read a titration curve
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket will ask you to use litmus results and to name a salt from its acid.

bullets: Vinegar stings a cut and tastes sharply sour, yet you can splash it on food
Laboratory hydrochloric acid is handled with gloves and goggles - so is every acid equally strong?
slides.heading: Sour but safe?
slides.notes: Ask the class: vinegar and hydrochloric acid are both acids, so why is one a food and the other a hazard? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because strength turns out to be about ions, not about the word acid.

bullets: Acids release H+ ions in water; alkalis release OH- ions in water
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline
Whichever ion is in excess decides the pH: more H+ means a lower pH, more OH- means a higher pH
slides.heading: One scale, two ion families
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: pH is an ion count. Every later scene - neutralisation, litmus, titration - is just the H+ and OH- counts changing.

bullets: Lemon juice and vinegar sit on the acid side; soap and baking soda sit on the alkali side
Chemists sort every solution on one number line: the pH scale
slides.heading: Acids and alkalis around you
slides.notes: Narrate the sorting as each item lands on the scale: familiar substances first, so the scale feels like a tool the class already half-knows.

bullets: The scale runs from 0 to 14 with 7 neutral in the middle
Each step away from 7 is ten times stronger, so pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4
slides.heading: The pH scale ladder
slides.notes: Climb the ladder one rung at a time and stress the ten-times jump at each rung: two rungs is not twice as strong, it is one hundred times.

bullets: An acid dissolved in water releases H+ ions; an alkali releases OH- ions
Count the ions: the one in excess sets the pH, and equal numbers mean neutral
slides.heading: What pH is really about: ions
slides.notes: Watch the ions appear as each substance dissolves. The pH is not a label stuck on the liquid - it is the score of a counting contest between two ion families.

bullets: H+ ions from the acid pair up with OH- ions from the alkali to make water
The leftover ions form a salt: acid plus alkali gives salt plus water
slides.heading: Neutralisation: a worked example
slides.notes: Follow one H+ ion and one OH- ion as they pair into a water molecule, then look at what is left floating: those leftover ions are the salt.

bullets: Blue litmus turns red in an acid; red litmus turns blue in an alkali
No colour change means the solution is neutral
slides.heading: The litmus test
slides.notes: Watch both papers dip and change. Keep the rule short enough to chant: blue to red means acid, red to blue means alkali.

bullets: The salt takes its second name from the acid: hydrochloric acid gives a chloride
Nitric acid gives a nitrate and sulfuric acid gives a sulfate
slides.heading: Naming the salt
slides.notes: Build each salt name from its acid on screen: the acid is the surname of the salt, so naming is a lookup, not a guess.

bullets: Strength is about how fully an acid releases its hydrogen ions, not about how sour or dangerous it feels
A weak acid only partly releases its hydrogen ions: vinegar is still acidic, just not strong
slides.heading: A common mistake: all acids are strong
slides.notes: Name the trap carefully before anyone falls into it: the word acid sounds dangerous, so students assume every acid ionises fully. Vinegar is the counterexample - acidic, but only partly ionised.

bullets: Base added drop by drop moves the pH slowly at first, then one drop leaps it from 4 to 10
That vertical jump is the equivalence point, and an indicator must change colour somewhere on it
slides.heading: The titration curve: watch for the jump
slides.notes: Trace the curve as it draws itself and freeze at the jump: a single drop did that, which is why the indicator has to change colour on the jump and not before or after.

bullets: Step 1: hydrochloric acid releases H+ ions and sodium hydroxide releases OH- ions; the H+ and OH- ions pair up to make water
Step 2: the leftover sodium and chloride ions form the salt, and because the acid is hydrochloric the salt is a chloride: sodium chloride
slides.heading: Worked example: neutralise hydrochloric acid
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: first pair the ions into water, then let the leftovers and the acid name give you the salt.

bullets: Nitric acid is neutralised by potassium hydroxide. Name the salt formed and write the word equation
Careful - a classmate says vinegar is not really an acid because you can eat it. Explain, using hydrogen ions, why vinegar is still acidic
slides.heading: Your turn: name that salt
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for anyone calling vinegar neutral or not an acid. The fix is the ion picture: a weak acid has released only some of its hydrogen ions.

bullets: On your own: state what happens to blue litmus in an alkali, and name the salt made when sulfuric acid is neutralised
Watch out for the trap one last time: strength is about how fully the ions are released, not about the word acid itself
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap picture - every acid as a fully ionised burner - and the fix: strength is how fully the hydrogen ions are released. Collect the tickets as they leave.
